title: Asian Games Chief Calls Container Rooms 'Functional' as OCA Defends Scrapping Athletes' Village
excerpt: Organising committee president Hideaki Omura promised fixes as delegations complain of short beds, leaking huts and long waits — while the OCA says a traditional village would have been a costly white elephant.
body:
• Asian Games organising committee president Hideaki Omura called athlete accommodation "functional" and promised fixes as complaints mount days before the opening ceremony.
  • The Olympic Council of Asia defended scrapping the traditional Athletes' Village, saying it would have become a "white elephant" after the Games — cost estimates had doubled to ¥60 billion.
  • Instead, 17,000 athletes and officials are split across a cruise ship, container-style huts and hotels, drawing complaints of 14-hour check-in waits, beds too short for tall athletes, and flooding after record rain.
  • Indian athletes faced long waits for room allocation, with some names missing from registration lists for the Costa Serena cruise ship.

'Functional' rooms, growing anger

Accommodation for athletes at the Asian Games in Japan is "functional," and organisers are working to address a wave of complaints from disgruntled teams, organising committee president Hideaki Omura told AFP on Thursday, a day before the Games open in Nagoya. "If there are different opinions then we will respond to them appropriately," said Omura, who is also the governor of Aichi prefecture. "At this point, while we are responding to individual opinions, we have been improving everything as issues arise and we will continue to respond that way."

More than 17,000 competitors and officials are expected at the continent's biggest multi-sport event. In a bid to control costs, organisers abandoned the traditional Athletes' Village in favour of distributed lodging: the Italian cruise ship Costa Serena housing around 4,000 people, shipping-container-style huts at Nagoya's port for some 2,000, and commercial hotels for roughly 9,000.

A plan under strain

The arrangement has drawn immediate fire. South Korean officials branded the container huts the "worst ever," citing cramped quarters and beds too short for taller athletes — the beds measure just 1.95 metres, while basketball player Lee Hyun-jun stands 2.02 metres. His teammate Byeon Jun-hyeong posted a video on social media showing a leaking sink and soaked floor in his hut, captioned "Please help us." An official from another team told AFP he walked into the facility, took one look, and booked a hotel instead.

Indian athletes have had their own ordeal: rowers and shooters faced waits of up to 14 hours for room allocation on the Costa Serena, while Indian wushu players and coaches found their names missing from registration lists. Hundreds of athletes were briefly evacuated from the container accommodation last week when record rainfall lashed Nagoya. Accommodation manager Yuta Matsuo told Reuters the organisers were "fully aware of the dissatisfaction and concerns" and were "already taking concrete steps to improve the environment."

"Yes, the Athletes' Village is good to look at. But at the end of the day, we need to be practical."

— Husain Al-Musallam, Director General, Olympic Council of Asia

The white-elephant defence

The Olympic Council of Asia has now gone on the record defending the decision. An Athletes' Village would have left organisers with a white elephant after the closing ceremony, OCA Director General Husain Al-Musallam told reporters on Friday. Initial cost estimates for a village to house 15,000 competitors and officials doubled from ¥30 billion to ¥60 billion, forcing the rethink. "You build the Athletes' Village, you spend such amount of money, and then we need to see what's going to happen after the Games' closing ceremony," Al-Musallam said. "(Considering) the cost and size of the Games, we need to be a little bit flexible."

Tayyab Ikram, head of the OCA Coordination Commission for Aichi-Nagoya, echoed the point: "We don't want to leave a white elephant after the Games here." While the next two Asian Games in Doha and Riyadh will feature Athletes' Villages, Ikram said such a village is not a mandatory element of the event.

India's contingent in the middle of it

For India's athletes, the accommodation saga adds logistical stress to a campaign already underway — basketball and football competitions began before Saturday's opening ceremony. Shot putter Tajinderpal Singh Toor revealed Indian athletes had trained for the conditions by sleeping in shipping containers back home. "Preparing the mind ahead for such challenges helps any sportsperson, and that's what we are doing by getting accustomed to sleeping in containers," the 6-foot-4 athlete told reporters. India is defending its women's cricket gold and opens its men's cricket campaign next week.

What to watch

The true test comes after Saturday's opening ceremony, when the full contingent of 17,000 arrives and daily operations begin in earnest. Whether Omura's "improving everything as issues arise" approach can keep pace with 45 nations' delegations — and whether the complaints fade once competition takes centre stage — will define how the 20th Asian Games are remembered.
image_caption: Container-style accommodation units for athletes at the Aichi-Nagoya 2026 Asian Games. Organising committee president Hideaki Omura called the rooms 'functional' amid complaints about cramped quarters and short beds.
nri_angle: Indian athletes faced 14-hour waits and missing registrations at the Nagoya Games, and the accommodation row is unfolding just as India's teams begin their medal campaigns.
